claims.text: Structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoparticles is governed by the interplay of thermally activated atomic diffusion and environment-induced surface segregation.
A reducing atmosphere accelerates elemental segregation and local ordering relative to an inert atmosphere.
A reducing atmosphere causes phase decomposition to begin earlier than an inert atmosphere.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, nearly equiatomic, multimetallic solid solutions.
Temperature-dependent atomic diffusion promotes local compositional fluctuations and ordering.
Surface or interface segregation predisposes the nanoparticles to local compositional fluctuations and ordering.
Atomic mobility increases at elevated temperature.
Elements prone to oxidation or segregation migrate preferentially to nanoparticle surfaces or interfaces at elevated temperature.
Reducing conditions lower diffusion barriers through enhanced reactivity.
Lower diffusion barriers under reducing conditions accelerate surface segregation, ordering, and phase decomposition.
The corresponding structural transformations are less pronounced or delayed in an inert atmosphere.
Reducing-atmosphere nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier onset and greater extent of segregation and phase separation than inert-atmosphere nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles annealed in an inert atmosphere will retain the initial solid-solution state to a higher temperature than those annealed in a reducing atmosphere.
The initial uniform solid-solution baseline applies below 473 K and under inert conditions.
Changes in particle size, composition, or environmental impurities may alter the atmosphere-dependent stability response.
Segregation and ordering thresholds can vary with the specific alloy system.
A lack of statistically significant atmosphere-dependent differences in segregation or ordering would falsify the proposed role of atmosphere.
